speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In other words, we reap what we sow, and the lifestyle decisions we make have a significant impact on our health in later life.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We cannot choose our parents and so our genetic make-up is predetermined, but we can certainly choose how we live our lives.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Likewise, as a nation, decisions we now make regarding our healthcare framework will have deep and far-reaching consequences on the healthcare landscape of the future.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Singapore we should take some credit for always keeping a constant eye on the future.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have all heard about SkillsFuture and other forward-looking policies, and healthcare is no exception.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since my earliest speeches about health and healthcare in this House during the Budget Debates, the Ministry of Health (MOH) has progressed its Healthcare Masterplan, first to 2020, then beyond 2020, and now onto 2030.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is great that we are planning for the future, but in order to future-proof the health of our citizens, we need to pay close attention to the present.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Shaping lifestyle decisions, ensuring a clean living environment and further improving socioeconomic conditions through inclusive growth remain arguably the most powerful means of influencing the health of our country.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That is why many studies have shown an inconstant correlation between healthcare spending and the overall health status of a country, since healthcare spending primarily captures the magnitude of expenditure on medical care, rather than the sum of efforts directed towards health maintenance.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that MOH will be able to provide an update to this House as to what progress has been made in encouraging Singaporeans to keep active and live healthily.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We still pride ourselves on being able to support a world-class medical care system and achieve world-class health standards, but it is increasingly becoming a stretch to declare that we can do so at a modest price.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of the big issues that has dominated this year's Budget is concerning the rise in the price of water.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Healthcare, like water, is a necessity and it is a public good.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of the measures that has been suggested to impress on the public the importance and true cost of water is to reintroduce rationing exercises.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I certainly am not suggesting that we consider rationing healthcare to encourage more judicious use of medical care, although I do note with consternation that there are countries, both developed and developing, which are actually seriously exploring various ways of rationing healthcare to their population as costs have ballooned out of control.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But we have to act now to rein in healthcare spending and channel resources to policies which have a proven impact on the health status of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are critical to the sustainability and future-proofing of our healthcare system, and I would like to ask what the Ministry has done to begin these shifts.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the past few years, we have made great progress in providing quality, affordable and accessible medical care, but the challenges to the health of Singaporeans remain formidable.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The emphasis on healthy eating is particularly laudable, since studies have shown that children who learn to eat healthily tend to continue to do so in their adult lives and are likely to pass on such habits to their children.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would surely be a significant pre-emptive strike in our continuing battle against diabetes and other chronic diseases.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that the Ministry could go even further by perhaps looking at legislation and enshrining such good practices in the requisite laws, such as what the United States (US) has done with the Healthy Hunger-Free Kids Act, which also addresses another issue, which is, to ensure that no child should start the school day without having a healthy breakfast.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also commend the announced focus on safeguarding sleep for our children.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does the Ministry intend to help parents and caregivers achieve the sleep goals for their children?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to recognise the steady investment the Ministry has made over the years in intermediate and long-term care (ILTC) and end-of-life care, both in terms of manpower and infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The disruptive effects of these advances will lead to new paradigms of healthcare delivery, and Singapore should be ready to embrace these shifts as they could lead to significant improvements in our well-being and can also be an impetus for economic development.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this generation, it is quite probable that medical care will become highly personalised, such that the care patients receive becomes more targeted, more efficient, safer and, ultimately, more affordable.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Personalised healthcare, also known as precision medicine, holds great promise for the future of healthcare.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Precision medicine refers to the ability to "tailor therapies to a patient's individual needs by examining their individual characteristics".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many countries are actively developing their capabilities here.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The US has its Precision Medicine Initiative, Europe has its European Alliance for Personalised Medicine, and China announced a massive investment in Personalised Medicine as part of its 13th Five-year Plan.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, this brave new world of medical therapy will have to be carefully navigated, and regulators will need to keep up.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Traditional systems of healthcare delivery will change, such as what defines a hospital, and can treatment only come from the more traditional medical institutions?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How do we make sense of the barrage of new technology and treatments and curate them properly for the benefit of our citizens?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have previously asked for a more robust framework for evaluating healthcare therapies, as there are many cautionary tales if one just looks around.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The sad stories of dubious therapies like alkaline water treatment, spectacular failures like that of the flawed or perhaps even fraudulent blood testing technology of Theranos are but some examples.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This means that we have to invest prudently and sustainably in the present and have a pragmatic roadmap for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One of the aims of Healthcare 2020 was to offer seamless, hassle-free and holistic care for patients across different stages of their healthcare journey.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With an ageing population, the need for primary and geriatric care will rise, relative to acute care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given the profile and needs of the aged and the already heavy load on our healthcare system, community-based healthcare is important and the pace of implementation has to pick up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given this, could the Ministry share what it has done and will continue to do to shift the centre of care to the community?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And in this digital age and in this Budget where we talk about digitalisation, could the Ministry also share how it has embraced technology to improve efficiency of healthcare delivery and to improve patients' access to healthcare within the community?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the years, we have put in place, streamlined and updated our healthcare systems and structures so as to keep pace with developments and needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Healthcare in Singapore has made many improvements and won international recognition.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking ahead, we must look beyond ensuring access, cost containment and convenience − all of which are still important − but also consider how we can deliver value-based healthcare, where health outcomes are maximised per dollar spent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As such, could MOH share what are its vision and plan beyond Healthcare 2020 and what it has done to achieve value-based healthcare?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could MOH share the desired outcomes that it wishes to attain for Singapore's healthcare system and population, as well as the key indicators that are being tracked?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is crucial that we plan ahead, in tandem with the expected ageing population, to ensure that we have the necessary infrastructure and manpower to meet the present and future healthcare needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In recent years, the construction of hospitals and medical centres has been ramped up, resulting in significant increases in the development expenditure of MOH.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Yet, according to a report published by the Lien Foundation and the Khoo Chwee Neo Foundation, the Government's efforts to ramp up capacity lags behind the rate at which the population is ageing.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Is this sufficient to cope with projected demand?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In early 2016, in a reply to a Parliamentary Question filed by my colleague, our doctor and nurse to population ratios still lag behind other developed countries, such as Australia, Japan, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The intention is to better optimise resources and provide more comprehensive and patient-centred care services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Each cluster will provide the full range of acute hospital care, primary care and community care and also include a medical school.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: However, a number of my patients and residents have expressed concern that if their preferred polyclinic and Government hospital are not within the same clusters, they will encounter problems after the regrouping is completed in 2018.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I had reassured them that under the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) system, our hospitals, specialist outpatient clinics and polyclinics have access to their medical records.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: In fact, they can also access them through the HealthHub system.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: So, it is quite seamless and they will not be adversely affected.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: However, this explanation was not fully satisfactory for them as some of them could not understand the necessity of the regrouping in the first place.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Ministry share in greater detail about the new healthcare system regrouping and, ultimately, how Singaporeans will benefit from this reorganisation?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: In what ways will the new system be more suitable for our future healthcare needs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: She has complicated diabetes and has to follow up with her diabetologist for sugar control; her podiatrist for her long-term foot ulcer; an ophthalmologist for her diabetes which has affected her eyes; and her worsening kidney function requires her to see a renal physician.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Some of her appointments are six-monthly and others are two- to three-monthly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Each visit will require her to collect medications from the pharmacist as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: To get to the specialist outpatient clinic or polyclinic, her daughter and son need to take turns off work, or her domestic helper will assist when they are overseas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: She will take a taxi usually but, a few times, she has had to have a non-emergency ambulance to send her to the facility which, of course, costs her more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Care coordination is the deliberate organisation of patient care activities to facilitate appropriate delivery of services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It will help our patients negotiate the system efficiently and effectively and, of course, it will also save them time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There is a need to address the potential gaps in meeting patients' interrelated medical, social, educational, as well as support services needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Too many transitions that exist today can, indeed, be confusing and time-consuming, especially for our seniors, and we are going to see more of them in the coming years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Care coordination has been identified as the key strategy by the US Institute of Medicine to increase effectiveness and safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How can we streamline and coordinate, as well as integrate these various types of services so that someone like as Mdm A can be in one place and all the disciplines can see her there, more along the lines of perhaps a medical mall, but not at private sector costing.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I believe this is partly due to doctors prescribing drugs for a long duration or prescribing non-standard drugs.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Two years ago, the Workers' Party (WP) suggested that the Government look into publishing drug prices for public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Next, under the National Childhood Immunisation Programme, all recommended vaccinations are fully subsidised and provided free of charge at all polyclinics for children who are Singapore Citizens, except pneumococcal vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Pneumococcal disease manifests in illnesses, such as pneumonia and meningitis, and is the leading infectious cause of death in children and adults worldwide.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: According to MOH's figures, pneumonia is the second most common cause of death in Singapore and one of the top five conditions of hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I understand that pneumococcal meningitis is a disease that is difficult to detect in the early stages but progresses rapidly and could result in death or cause long-term health complications, such as paralysis or brain damage.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Children below five years old and adults above 50 are at greater risk of being affected by such a disease.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I ask MOH to consider providing a subsidy to encourage parents to use it.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I believe that the Government stands to benefit from providing subsidised pneumococcal vaccinations in the long run through the reduced burden on MediSave and MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It could also save on expensive treatments, hospitalisations and medications down the line.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am appealing to MOH to implement a grace period for the withdrawal or reduction of subsidies instead of effecting the changes immediately when the per capita household income rises.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the current framework, a Singapore Citizen will qualify for 75% subsidies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a 15% decrease, which is considerable, especially since we are talking about Singaporeans with lower household per capita monthly income.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would apply even if their income only rose by about 10% to $710.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Singaporeans who are at the receiving end, this can be very discouraging and could feel like two steps forward, one step back.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A grace period should be given before the subsidy is withdrawn or reduced.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will give people some breathing room to consolidate their finances or even pay off some lingering debts, instead of hitting them with an immediate cost increase for medical expenses.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: One was a medical bill and the other was a Central Provident Fund (CPF) statement of her 91-year-old parent.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: She was asking me, "My parent is 91 years old.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Why can the Government not allow her to deduct a bit more from her MediSave?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We do have our MediSave, we can help her out, too, but why do you need us to still use cash to make payment?" I know that the Government has already introduced Flexi-MediSave for the elderly.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Government further enhance this Flexi-MediSave for the elderly to allow for a further increase, perhaps a 20% increase, in claim limit for MediSave for hospitalisation, surgery and treatment?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For our elderly patients, the systemic rehabilitation programmes offered by community hospitals help to improve their functional abilities and quality of life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should do what we can to increase accessibility to such services at community hospitals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo referred to this as "right-siting" in his speech last week in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Paradoxically, our healthcare financing scheme may stand in the way of such a development.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I propose that direct admission patients in community hospitals be allowed to utilise MediShield Life for their inpatient treatments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is no need for acute hospitals to act as a filter.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I am glad that ElderShield will be enhanced soon.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I first spoke on ElderShield in May 2002, several months before its implementation.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, this is the 11th time I am speaking on this topic in this House.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Before its implementation in 2002, I already raised concerns about its inadequacy with payouts of $300 over a tenure of five years.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These patients with three Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) are totally dependent on others for their daily living.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: A payout pegged to the amount required for engaging a full-time domestic helper will be more appropriate.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I am not suggesting that such full-time assistance be a norm.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These patients with three ADLs, especially those as a result of old age, are unlikely to get back to normal if they have reached the stage of inability to perform the daily activities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: But even for other sick patients with severe disability due to sicknesses, such as stroke or cancer, to reach the stage of not being able to perform three daily activities will usually mean that their illnesses are too severe for them to revert to normal activities again.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, the insurance coverage of five to six years will leave them in a lurch at the end when their needs usually increase rather than decrease and they need even more dependent care at higher costs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is necessary because of our society's fast-ageing population and smaller families.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Through bigger economies of scale, a universal scheme will help make this insurance viable in the long run.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Everyone should be included, regardless of age and prevailing medical conditions, just like in MediShield Life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The MediShield premium is affordable because there are subvention and subsidy, especially for those with lower income.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope ElderShield premiums will be made affordable, too.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Considering that the disability prevalence rate presently is about 5% for those 65 years and above, it means there are already some 15,000 people requiring aged care facility per year.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, 13,000 claimants for ElderShield over 15 years is actually a small number.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This may be due to ElderShield's onerous eligibility of three out of five ADLs for claims.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Enhanced ElderShield is important to reduce the dependence on institutional care unnecessarily as well as providing right-siting.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Presently, some families take the option of sending their dependent members to community hospitals or overstaying in acute hospitals to save on dependent care cost, as there is subvention for hospital and institutional care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The present ElderShield excludes those 70-year-olds in 2002 and those with existing illnesses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These are the people who are more likely to get severe disability and be badly in need of the ElderShield but are excluded for this insurance.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many seniors are not in the scheme because they cannot afford these premium amounts.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope the Enhanced ElderShield will include this group with affordable premiums.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: MediShield has been revamped to the superior MediShield Life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps MOH will now consider revamping ElderShield to ElderShield Life, similar to MediShield Life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The many new features of MediShield Life had been well thought out and they are very good.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It will be good if MOH could consider adopting them similarly to ElderShield Life with inclusion of its lifelong coverage, its universal feature and its permanent subsidy in premiums for seniors, low-income Singaporeans and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope MOH will consider my suggestions above in reviewing ElderShield and to make ElderShield the true safety net that it is intended to be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: ElderShield is meant to be a Severe Disability Insurance scheme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, payouts are only for 72 months, and I understand that a quarter of claimants outlive this and still need care.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Ministry consider making payouts for life?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, premiums are also higher for women than it is for men.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Insurance is supposed to pool risks across different life expectancies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, will the Ministry make the premiums equal for men and women?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And even then, the subsidies only apply for the procedures and public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some research state that clinically relevant facility decline is in for women aged 41 to 42.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry consider extending the qualifying age for subsidies to 42?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the subsidies also be extended to treatments at private hospitals so as to reduce waiting time?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We have a strong focus on urging Singaporeans to start a family and trying to assist those who are not ready to start a family yet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We currently only provide the co-funding for treatments done at public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The success rate at private hospitals or clinics may be higher.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As such, I hope we can extend the co-funding for the last fresh cycle to be done at private hospitals and clinics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This will help couples who have tried repeatedly at public hospitals and have not been able to have a successful pregnancy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This will also help alleviate the large demand for ART treatments at our public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Pay for Success contracting (PFS) and Social Impact Bonds (SIBs) have been growing worldwide since 2010.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One estimate has identified over 40 SIB and PFS projects worldwide in 2015, spanning subject areas like early childhood education, healthcare and recidivism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Israel, an SIB is underway to help prevent pre-diabetics from contracting diabetes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Singapore, MOH could explore launching an SIB to raise funds for reliable non-government organisation (NGO) partners who can then work with pre-diabetics and diabetics to improve health indicators like blood sugar levels and emergency hospitalisation events.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Philanthropic donors, foundations and so on could buy the bond.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such NGOs could then use the bond proceeds to fund programmes to help at-risk individuals manage their diets, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The state would redeem the bond and pay the donors only if outcomes are achieved, which makes for better use of state monies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NGOs may be better placed than state entities to dream up and execute creative ideas that can nudge behavioural change in the face of entrenched habits, thus solving tricky social problems.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that MOH will look into the possibility of launching an SIB or PFS initiative to work with NGOs over the social challenge of diabetes.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Our children and young people are increasingly overweight.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: One in three Singaporeans has a lifetime risk of developing diabetes, with serious and costly consequences.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister give us a report of the progress from the front?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: On sugary processed food, would the Government consider requiring warnings on containers of sugary processed food, such as cans and packets of candies, soft drinks and so on?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This could be similar to requiring warnings on tobacco packaging in order to discourage smoking, which is another risk factor for diabetes.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Smokers are 30%-40% more likely to develop diabetes.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, would the Government consider requiring retailers to display signs that encourage shoppers to choose low-sugar options, or school canteens and hawker centres to display signs warning about the dangers of diabetes and encouraging low-sugar options?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Would the Minister consider working with the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) to apply existing incentives to support local food manufacturers to release low-sugar snacks and drinks?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to the US Renal Data System Report last year, Singapore leads the world in the percentage of kidney failures caused by diabetes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides kidney failure, diabetes is also associated with heart attack and stroke.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because of the high social and financial costs that diabetes has on the individual Singaporean, his family and society, war was declared on diabetes in April last year.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister provide an update on the programmes that it has recently introduced to combat diabetes, especially in terms of healthy diet initiatives and proposed regular exercise regimes?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ultimately, the war on diabetes is something we have to fight together and the best cure for it is prevention.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This is a suggestion, going forward, to improve the care of our seniors with a sustainable solution.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: MOH has been adopting the adage "prevention is better than cure" over the years to manage many chronic health diseases like diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Thus, let us aim for seniors to age gracefully with independent living in their own homes despite their frailty or medical conditions by preventing disabilities and to better manage any disabilities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many older adults express the desire to "age-in-place" for as long as possible and prefer to live at home rather than being admitted to nursing homes or community hospitals.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Such cluster homes enable daily service delivery convenience.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: These cluster homes will have elderly-smart home concepts that embrace accessible designs and environmental modifications to foster independent living and to improve the occupant's functional ability-related outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could the various Ministries work hand in hand towards this end?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Thus, it would be good if there is collaboration between MOH and the Ministry of National Development (MND) in co-planning "smart cluster homes" for seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The seniors in such cluster homes can be provided with daily needs with assistance from helpers and even medical personnel when necessary.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The ground floors of such homes should be used for community services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Hence, "Seniors Activity Centres" to enable those well seniors to come down daily for physical, social and mental wellness programmes would be ideal.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Such venues will also serve as coordinating centres that enable concept partners like the grassroots organisations, VWOs and various corporations to volunteer their services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MOH collaborate with the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) to provide seamless assistance to those seniors who require financial and social needs in these cluster homes?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Senior Care Centres (SCCs) for residents and coordinating centres for volunteers at the void decks of cluster homes can be managed by MSF.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: MOH can provide training, like ability to pick up tell-tale signs of suicidal thoughts, for the befriender volunteers that MSF manages.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Again, collaboration among Ministries is important for better identification of needy residents and the delivery of assistance and outreach.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Such collaboration will also prevent duplication of services or over-servicing to some residents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Does MOH have any charting of roadmaps for the care of seniors?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: There is a need for this to better plan for the delivery of services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: For instance, it helps to know where the places with the highest concentration of seniors are, what the age group of seniors who require most assistance and the types of assistance they require.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: There is also a need to know the number of cases with medical conditions, such as chronic diseases, physical disabilities, dementia and other mental illnesses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This will enable better planning, especially in the area of medical personnel, towards catering for these conditions.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Do we have enough geriatricians, physiotherapists, community doctors and hospice-care doctors?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: We do need more community medical personnel that can visit patients in their homes in order to provide good homecare.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: We should train more medical workers using shorter course modules as in wound dressings, change of catheters or nasogastric tubes and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: In England, medical workers are trained in just months to accomplish these tasks.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Does MOH have enough dieticians to help in the fight against diabetes?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Dieticians are also needed to advise all centres, especially the Seniors Activity Centres, that provide food for groups of people to ensure healthy diets.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The use of medical technology to improve quality of living is the way forward.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Does MOH have a designated team or department to look into the availability, applications and effectiveness of medical technological devices that can enable better healthcare monitoring, especially for elderly care, and test them on their effectiveness?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Does MOH have collaborative partnerships with Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to develop new technology, while researching and developing cost-effective systems that promote an age-friendly living environment in homes?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MOH step up the healthcare awareness and promotion for prevention of chronic diseases, osteoporosis, heart diseases and mental illnesses among women?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Is there a target for achievement and what else can be done to get a better outcome to reduce problems faced by women in combating ill-health?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Can there be a more ground-up approach that involves corporations and community groups to get better outreach to the wider audience?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As highlighted in the Masterplan, we, as a community, must recognise that caregivers are individuals with their own aspirations and ambitions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: While family is the first and most important line of support, family caregivers can only carry out their roles effectively if they are emotionally and physically well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This was a point carried in the Enabling Masterplan 3 Report.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This problem may be more acute for caregivers of persons with mental disabilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hence, we see the current focus to build capacity for home-based and community-based care services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Where caregivers of persons with mental disabilities do not have access to such services, the care responsibility falls solely and squarely on them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They, therefore, suffer tremendous stress and may even feel overwhelmed by the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This issue is even more acute where the caregiver is the primary breadwinner and has to juggle employment and worry about finances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Caregivers for such persons face the same, if not more, pressure as compared to caregivers of persons with physical disabilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There should be no distinction between these groups.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I made the same point during my Adjournment Motion last year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I understand that the relevant agencies are still studying this issue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would be grateful, therefore, if the Ministry could share some of its plans for greater home-based support and to give caregivers of persons with mental disabilities more opportunities for respite.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The stress of caregiving goes up exponentially when the elderly develop chronic illnesses, dementia or disabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I propose that the Government set up similar caregiver support centres for senior caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As senior caregiving is of a scale larger than disability caregiving, I believe that there is a need to set up multiple support centres to provide the same level of support to senior caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These centres are a natural extension to the existing SCCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since SCCs are specially situated in places with higher demand for eldercare services, Senior Caregiver Support Centres can be co-located with SCCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like the Disability Caregiver Support Centre, Senior Caregiver Support Centres can provide information, planned respite, training, peer support and offer various VWO programmes to help caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is one more important function the support centres can perform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior caregivers face greater risk of health and financial vulnerabilities as they get older due to lower lifetime earnings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many are women who leave the workforce to be full-time caregivers and who find it difficult to re-enter the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These support centres can also act as the main touchpoints for caregivers to receive important health and financial assistance and even advice on finding part-time work to support themselves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This is not the most suitable model to enhance the quality of life for our seniors who are residing in these homes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Do each of us want to live in such an environment in the winter of our lives?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We should move away from the dormitory-like environment, go beyond basic physical care to a home-like environment with care specialists attending to the social well-being as well as nursing needs of elderly residents so that they can live and age with dignity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: MOH should consult as many stakeholders as possible, as well as the specific medical interest groups most associated with the care of patients afflicted with specific illnesses, such as the Alzheimer's Disease Association, Kidney Dialysis Foundation and so on, in order to better understand how the clinical and social needs of different and specific types of patients can be best met.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This would allow for a range, rather than a bare minimum standard, of care in each nursing home.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Recently, a Fengshan resident shared with me her concern to transfer her mother from one nursing home to another, and one of the reasons cited was poor and indifferent care by staff.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I understand that, right now, the Ministry conducts regular audits on nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: However, the audit reports are not disclosed to the public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I believe that such measures may enhance standards and weed out operators who are not able to provide suitable services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I had spoken about digital eldercare in last year and this year's Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Digital eldercare offers many possibilities and has many applications.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Today, I would just like to focus on how it can enable independent living and better match demand to the supply of eldercare services and how we can facilitate this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Let us reserve institutional care for those who need very highly intensive care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We should leverage more on technology, such as sensors, assistive devices and telemedicine, to enable independent living at home, even for those who have moderate disabilities and little or no family support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: There are already pilots being done with the deployment of the Elderly Monitoring System (EMS), for example.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could the Ministry update the House on the results and key learning points from these pilots?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could the Government take a point position and lead a nationwide implementation of smart homes for seniors?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could the Ministry facilitate the integration of these solutions so that the elderly can enjoy the services at home in an easy and seamless manner?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We need to enable them to age in a very holistic conceptual manner if we were to have smart homes for seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Next, digital platforms are now available to link freelance healthcare professionals and caregivers to facilitate on-demand provision of home care or other related eldercare services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But some of these platforms are privately run and the elderly who wish to utilise them may be deterred for fear that the subsidies they may be eligible for cannot be applied via these platforms.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last year, we declared war here in this Chamber, War on Diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I also highlighted three key shifts we need to make to prepare ourselves for the future beyond 2020.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, I will give an update on the progress of Healthcare 2020, as requested by Dr Chia Shi-Lu.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I will also give Members an update on the state of the War on Diabetes and outline our broad strategies to achieve the three key shifts beyond 2020.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: My colleagues will then elaborate on the specific efforts and the measures we intend to include.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have also made progress in managing and treating diseases which are leading causes of premature death for Singaporeans, such as ischaemic heart disease and stroke.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our obesity prevalence rate has risen to 1.7 times, a 70% increase, from 1992 to 2013.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is worrying as obesity is a key driver contributing to the diabetes burden in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Obesity and diabetes are risk factors for heart disease and stroke.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we do not address these risk factors early, the progress on these two diseases will be eroded.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We, therefore, have a strong impetus to keep our Singaporeans healthy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Allow me to give an update on Healthcare 2020.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Since 2012, we have opened Ng Teng Fong General Hospital (NTFGH), Changi General Hospital Integrated Building (CGH IB), Jurong Community Hospital (JCH) and Yishun Community Hospital (YCH).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Next year, Changi General Hospital will open its new Medical Centre, which will allow it to expand its specialist outpatient services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also expect to open the Sengkang General and Community Hospitals by end-2018.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The new National Centre for Infectious Diseases is also due to open progressively from end-2018.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The construction of Outram Community Hospital is underway and it is scheduled to open by 2020.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is part of our overall plan to redevelop the Outram Campus, including the Singapore General Hospital, in a multi-phase process that will take us up to 20 years or more.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Woodlands General Hospital and its co-located community hospital will break ground next month and they will be opened progressively from 2022.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The National University Health System (NUHS) will take over the operations of Alexandra Hospital after the Sengkang team, which is currently in Alexandra Hospital, moves to the new Sengkang hospital in 2018.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The 79-year-old Alexandra Campus is a unique site.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The campus offers a unique opportunity as it has tremendous potential for redevelopment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I have, therefore, tasked NUHS to re-imagine healthcare for the future, taking the opportunity to design new and innovative care models that can better promote health and integrate care, and test them out at the Alexandra Campus.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In addition to hospital developments, we have added seven new Family Medicine Clinics (FMCs) and seven Community Health Centres (CHCs) to support the primary care GPs in the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have also added 3,400 nursing home beds and 5,600 centre-based care and home care places since 2012.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will add another 4,200 beds and 4,700 places by 2020.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But adding capacity alone is not a sustainable solution in the long term if we do nothing else.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our capacity growth must be coupled with efforts to transform our care model to leverage on strong primary and community care and keep our people healthy with better disease prevention and healthier lifestyle choices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To deliver quality services to our people, we need to grow and develop our healthcare manpower.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The healthcare workforce has expanded by some 23,000 or 33% over the past five years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need 9,000 more healthcare workers over the next three years, and there are many good career opportunities for Singaporean professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Given Singapore's limited labour pool, however, we cannot just grow the number but ensure that our healthcare workers are meaningfully and effectively deployed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will share more about MOH's efforts to build a strong, future-ready healthcare workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Several Members have asked about the affordability of healthcare.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have a multi-layer system of support to ensure that Singaporeans can afford the appropriate care that they need.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Treatment and drugs that are clinically effective and cost-effective are subsidised.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Means-tested Government subsidies at hospitals, Specialist Outpatient Clinics, CHAS clinics and nursing homes serve as the baseline support.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Larger bills, such as inpatient hospital bills and selected costly outpatient bills like chemotherapy and kidney dialysis, are covered by MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Since its launch in late 2015, MediShield Life has provided Singaporeans and, especially the seniors, with better support and assurance.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Claims by older Singaporeans aged above 65 increased even more, at 73% from 124,000 to 215,000 claims.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This resulted in a 90% jump in the total amount of claims for seniors from $181 million to $343 million.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about MediShield Life coverage for direct admissions to community hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As an extension of this coverage, MediShield Life covers community hospital stays for patients transferred from acute hospitals to community hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Nonetheless, we note there could be some groups of patients who are suitable for direct admission to community hospitals without going through acute hospitals and might benefit from MediShield Life coverage.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will study this proposal carefully because it has impact on premiums as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: After subsidies and MediShield Life, the patient can use his MediSave savings to cover his share of the healthcare bills.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked if the Flexi-MediSave limits could be raised.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So far, the majority of eligible patients have not fully utilised their Flexi-MediSave withdrawal limits.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is still early days, but it suggests that the claim limits are generally sufficient.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang asked about profit margins for our drugs in our hospitals and public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I should take this opportunity to clarify that our public healthcare institutions are not-for-profit organisations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While the drug prices include a margin, this is to offset overheads and operation costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, they are not profit margins; they are just margins to cover part of operation costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In addition, the Medications Assistance Fund (MAF) is also available to help patients with selected high-cost non-standard drugs, if it is deemed necessary.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Patients who still face difficulties despite all these subsidies can also apply for MediFund.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With Government subsidies and the 3Ms, MediShield Life, MediFund and MediSave, Singaporeans have multiple layers of support for their healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The system is constantly evolving and we will regularly review the adequacy of drug subsidies and the different schemes to ensure that medication remains affordable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While we have made steady progress on Healthcare 2020, we need to plan for the long term.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last year, I outlined our plans to go beyond Healthcare 2020, encapsulated in the "3 Beyonds".

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to move beyond hospital to the community; move beyond quality to value; and move beyond healthcare to health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These three moves are critical in preparing us to meet our long-term healthcare needs in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The first step is to better organise ourselves so that we can implement these three shifts more decisively and effectively.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With the reorganisation, the three integrated clusters will each have a broader range of healthcare services and facilities that will provide our patients with more seamless care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They can also tap on a larger pool of resources, including manpower and talent, both professional and managerial talent.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The integrated clusters can also offer healthcare workers greater development and training opportunities, thereby raising the competency of our workers that will translate into better quality of care and, eventually, benefit our patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Primary care will play an increasingly important role in our care transformation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is why we are strengthening the primary care capabilities of each cluster.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The National University Polyclinics (NUP) will be created under NUHS.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With this move, each cluster will now have its own polyclinic group.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This will enable the clusters to work in close collaboration with the GPs to augment our primary care sector and partner a wider range of community-based service providers, including VWOs, to anchor care firmly in the community, as pointed out by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister of State Lam Pin Min will share more about our plans in the primary care sector, including partnerships with the private GPs, through the Primary Care Networks scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will speak on our plans to strengthen our community mental health capabilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister of State Chee Hong Tat will share about our collaboration with our community partners.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Another area of emphasis for us is to go beyond quality and offer patients value in healthcare provision.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Advancements in medicine and healthcare technology offer new opportunities and potential for health and healthcare in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We want to keep abreast of such developments so that we can introduce new solutions that are clinically effective and cost-efficient and improve healthcare outcomes and quality of life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As pointed out by Dr Chia Shi-Lu, we must be mindful that newer does not always mean better.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some new drugs or treatments may not offer significant clinical advantage and, yet, come at a significantly higher cost.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Generic drugs often offer similar outcomes as branded drugs, but at fraction of the cost.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A good example would be the generic drugs for statins, used to manage high blood cholesterol, which usually cost less than half the price of the branded versions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Opting for generic drugs will help to reduce medication cost and we are working with our doctors to promote the use of generic drugs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Through the work of ACE, we aim to identify treatments with good outcomes at affordable costs to guide our doctors and patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister of State Lam will also share how ACE's work on Appropriate Care Guides will play an important role in our war on diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Moving beyond hospital to community, and beyond quality to value, are about how we change and improve the way we deliver healthcare to our patients who are already ill.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But what is perhaps even more important and critical is to nurture a healthy nation and a healthy people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is why our third thrust is on moving beyond healthcare to health, focusing on early interventions and healthy lifestyle choices which will keep people in good health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is easy to say but hard to do.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have several initiatives on this, which my colleagues will elaborate later.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Chen Show Mao have asked about the progress of our War on Diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These are underpinned by public education, data analytics and research as well as the mobilisation of stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The taskforce has engaged widely over the last six months and made useful recommendations even as their work continues.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: My colleagues will elaborate on these recommendations later on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I will focus on how we can win this war, by working together with communities, businesses, employers, workers and individuals, you and me.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And we are doing so through initiatives, such as the Community Networks for Seniors (CNS) which we launched last year.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our aim is to bring CNS to more mature communities progressively so that we can make every community a place where our seniors can be cared for and supported by the community to age well in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Advisors and Members of Parliament (MPs), too, can play an active part in helping to spread the message and keep their residents healthy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister Lim Swee Say, for example, has set up a diabetes taskforce in Bedok to raise awareness on diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I visited one of his many Chit Chat sessions last week, where he personally shared about the War on Diabetes with about 50 residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is a lot of hard work, but there is no short cut.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All of us have to play our part, in our own way, to reach out to our residents, to help them stay healthy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Not just in the community, at the workplaces, too.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Seagate Technology International's Woodlands office is one such example.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They regularly organise activities for their staff and participated in the National Steps ChallengeTM Season 2 Corporate Challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The office even organised an "intra-organisation challenge" to motivate their employees to clock more steps.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Their efforts have paid off as I was told that all their participants have an average daily step count of more than 10,000 steps.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Seagate Woodlands is also one of the top scorers for the Corporate Challenge!

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I look forward to more employers coming on board this War on Diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: After all, a healthy workforce is a prerequisite for a productive workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To fight this war, and to fight any war, we need soldiers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As individuals, we can play a part by being responsible for the choices that we make every day.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Apart from staying active, it is also important that we watch our diet.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A healthy diet is half a battle won, as we say.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Many of us eat out regularly, and that is why MOH and the Health Promotion Board (HPB) have also been actively engaging our hawker centres, coffee shops and restaurants to offer healthier meals with lower calories and beverages with lower sugar.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Like Minister Lim, I, too, share with my residents tips to combat diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I encourage them to follow the three "R's" − Refrain, Reduce and Replace.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: When we decide what to eat, Refrain from unhealthy food, if you can.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If you cannot but have to eat, try to Reduce the amount of unhealthy food that you have to eat.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If you cannot Refrain and cannot Reduce the amount, then please Replace with healthier alternatives.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In Mandarin):   For those who are at risk of developing diabetes, or who already have the disease, we need to help them manage their condition and prevent complications.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last year, we introduced diabetes roadshows, talks and screenings in the community, and reached more than 120,000 people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In addition, we also have HPB's Diabetes Prevention Programme which helps those with slightly elevated blood sugar levels reverse their risk for diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: She frequently encourages her friends to go for beverages with less or no sugar, and to choose healthier meal options.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: She also participates in the physical activities at Agape Village.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In English): Madam, in my Mandarin speech, I shared the story of Mdm Goh who benefited from HPB's Diabetes Prevention Programme, which helped her manage her blood sugar level and prevent diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Programmes like these are useful in helping pre-diabetics better manage their conditions through healthy eating and exercise habits.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The War on Diabetes will not be a quick battle and we must be prepared to keep up the momentum and go the distance.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to fight the war on the ground one day at a time, one battle at a time, and even one person at a time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Winning the war is not about building more hospitals and clinics to take care of those who are already ill.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to do so, but not only building them, but motivating Singaporeans to take charge of their health, to live their lives free of diabetes and, for those who already have diabetes, to provide them with support to help them to manage their conditions well.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The three key shifts − beyond hospital to community, beyond quality to value and beyond healthcare to health − will define the future direction of health and healthcare in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They will lead us towards good, affordable and sustainable healthcare in the long term.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All Singaporeans − you and me − want to have good health for themselves and for their family members.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, let us work together as one healthcare system to bring better care, better health and better life to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Of course, it also helps to foster stronger mental resilience within the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Grassroots leaders, hawkers, community partners and residents who are interested were all engaged and trained to equip them with useful information and skills so that they can offer timely assistance to residents with mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: However, the current set up is only effective if the elderly or their families approach us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Currently, we only know of the elderly who are identified through our local screening exercise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: There are others who are already diagnosed but may not be known to us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: For instance, instead of waiting to help a lost elderly, we can have befrienders and micro-community networks to reach out to and support elderly with dementia and their families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This continues to be a barrier to people wanting to seek help and also cause prejudice to deepen within the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: So, could the Ministry share what it is doing to combat the stigma, increase awareness and ensure that those who need help will get the help needed?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With our ageing population, the number of patients with mental health issues, such as dementia, is expected to rise.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope public education efforts will be stepped up to help raise our community's general knowledge of such conditions, so that we can better support the efforts of our health professionals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Community Mental Health (CMH) Masterplan is making good progress, especially in reaching out to patients to ensure they get more community support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am particularly glad for the setting up of dementia-friendly communities and the Community Resource, Engagement and Support Teams (CREST).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to ask for a clearer framework to support residents dealing with instances of neighbours with mental health issues creating disturbances in the estate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Callers should be able to receive speedy responses after contacting dedicated 24-hour hotlines for help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does the Ministry ensure we have sufficient numbers of trained GPs in ageing estates?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The Minister estimated that this figure is expected to rise to 80,000 by 2030.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We are also starting to see growing numbers of younger dementia patients.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The rapid increase in the number of people with dementia is a cause for concern, especially if we do not have enough resources to support them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: As such, I would like to ask the Minister for an update on the progress in preparing for the rise in dementia cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Is enough being done to educate Singaporeans on the risk factors for dementia?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: There has been an initiative to build dementia-friendly communities in Singapore, piloted at Yishun, Hong Kah and MacPherson.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: These communities feature "community touchpoints" that act as go-to points for those who have lost their way, and training is provided to persons and businesses within the area so that they may render assistance to persons with dementia.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: What are the findings of this initiative so far, and how does it compare with plans to address dementia in other countries?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Are there plans to roll out this initiative island-wide; and, if so, what is the schedule for this?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I would also like to raise the issue of dementia assessments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Currently, dementia assessments are usually carried out at hospitals and the Institute of Mental Health (IMH).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Will the Ministry set a target to eventually have trained staff at all polyclinics to perform the assessment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: There are a variety of reasons why mental wellness and mental health issues are becoming more prominent in society and these are due to greater awareness, public education and, of course, our ageing population, among others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We are making positive moves in managing mental health issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Greater strengthening and coordination will help consolidate the many good initiatives which are already existing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This will really help to reinforce what we already have.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: It is with the aim of enhancing service delivery, standardisation of care with a shared mental model, appropriate skills mix in providers potentiated through relevant training, thus forming a multidisciplinary community of practice, as well as the inclusion of caregiver support and empowerment, and not forgetting also the preventive and educational part as well as the rehabilitative services for such patients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: With this, everyone involved in mental health care is aligned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: It is also a model that stresses on the multidimensional aspects of quality care required in mental health issues.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There are several issues which I wish to highlight with some suggestions.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: First, the manpower issues in primary care and step-down care.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With the growing need to address the intermediate and long-term needs of Singaporeans and to further strengthen our primary care sector via primary care network or community care services, the jobs of the future may well be from the ILTC sectors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The healthcare sector faces challenges filling the many job vacancies.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I encourage MOH to work with the Labour Movement which has set up a Future Jobs, Skills and Training (FJST) department to identify emerging opportunities in the job market across various sectors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Together with employers, FJST will determine the necessary expertise and training workers will need to join the healthcare industry.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry and FJST will then work in close collaboration to tailor relevant training courses which are supported by the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) Education and Training Fund.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To that, how can MOH facilitate the gathering and sharing of such data to best utilise funds for targeted training?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With a greater demand for manpower in the ILTC sector, how can we enhance the attractiveness of jobs in the industry through better wages and career progression?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As the ILTC sector grows its manpower, how do we ensure a strong Singaporean Core?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can the SkillsFuture programmes allow more to be equipped with the necessary skills to enter the industry?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There are many women in their 50s seeking employment and this can be a possible source of manpower to fill job vacancies in the ILTC sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that with the new Attach and Train programme as well as SkillsFuture funding support, we can better tap into this resource to address the manpower shortage issue.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Nurses play a major role in our healthcare system.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Besides the recommendations of the National Nursing Taskforce in 2014, does the Ministry have plans to develop the nursing workforce further?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we further improve the Singaporean Core in the nursing profession?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, encouraging to note that the Government supports modular and e-learning training.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How would MOH regulate certification required of healthcare staff with the move towards modular and e-learning?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How ready are MOH and the respective healthcare regulatory bodies in recognising modular learning and qualification?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How do we ensure that this does not erode the quality of care to patients?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The SkillsFuture Leadership Development Initiative which aims to help aspiring Singaporeans acquire leadership competencies and critical experiences can attract more young Singaporeans to join the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As we welcome the initiative, how can it be extended to the healthcare sector as part of leadership development for healthcare workers?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While offering more overseas training opportunities for nurses or allied healthcare professionals, how can we ensure that they return to Singapore to help build a stronger Singaporean Core with deeper capabilities?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This will be a well-coordinated effort which standardises training beyond the basics and provides a one-stop centre for courses and skills advancement.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With the support from MOM, the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i), NTUC Learning Hub and various IHL partnerships, the tripartite alliance academy for healthcare can help to meet the demand for a skilled workforce in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One would also understand that the lack of manpower and the reliance on foreign workers are inevitable unless the healthcare sector transforms itself to improve productivity and innovation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Through this, many improvements were made over the last five years as we embark on automation and improve processes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to align and standardise best practices for systems and processes to keep our healthcare system safe and affordable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The reorganisation is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I would also urge that MOH consider having health volunteers, health ambassadors to penetrate the community to address the need of an ageing population better and tapping into the pool of caregivers or domestic helpers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Healthcare expenditure and the demand for manpower are rising with our ageing population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, healthcare manpower and fiscal sustainability are critical for us to solve.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could MOH share what it is doing to ensure manpower and fiscal sustainability?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What innovations and productivity measures have been implemented and how have the gains from these measures helped improve sustainability?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Can the community and volunteers play a bigger role to address unfulfilled needs?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Has the Ministry identified the main reasons for these problems and what measures does it have to overcome these challenges?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: In addition, for foreigners recruited to help fill the manpower shortage, what measures does MOH have to ensure that they are sufficiently trained in our local system and our local culture so that they can deliver the desired quality of care?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I would also like to know if we are on track to train and recruit enough doctors and nurses for geriatric medicine and gerontology and how we can build a strong Singaporean Core for this group of specialists.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The confluence of information technology (IT), artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics will have a significant impact on healthcare.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Today, we are already deploying autonomous transporters, such as automated guided vehicles (AGV) and clean fix robots, in our healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: These and robotic-assisted beds and many other smart applications and machines will play an increasingly vital role in our hospitals and clinics.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I have no doubt that they will lead to higher quality services and gains in productivity.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: However, this would mean that we need a strong team of competent technical professionals to service, maintain and upgrade these sophisticated networks and machinery.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Ministry share how we can train and recruit these talents and keep them in this competitive global market?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With more than 30,000 jobs in the healthcare sector, the sector is poised to absorb many more workers, especially mid-career PMEs and workers who may be displaced or looking for an alternative career.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This includes women who are keen to return to work after having left the workforce to look after their children or care for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: PMEs who visit our NTUC U PME Centre lament to me that most of the PCP places for the healthcare sector have been taken up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, urge MOH to work with e2i and Workforce Singapore (WSG) to come up with new PCPs in more areas than the current offering and even more PCP places in view of the strong manpower demand.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On another note, I am excited to hear of the various expansion plans and new public healthcare institutions coming up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I am very concerned about how we can find the necessary manpower needed to staff these institutions, with the many productivity and technological interventions already in place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Allied health professionals, such as physiotherapists, dieticians and speech therapists, are important vocations which ease the load off doctors and nurses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Why not then formalise their training and continuing professional development through the vehicle of a new MOH-sponsored academy?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A well-trained and professional allied workforce benefits the patients immensely, eases the doctor's workload and, importantly, provides meaningful career opportunities for young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Why not introduce diploma and degree courses in our polytechnics and universities to build up a locally trained body of allied health professionals to meet the growing need for healthcare?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
