text: After these Singaporeans graduate, they can become members of an allied health academy, so as to keep abreast of latest developments and advancements in medicine, continue their professional development and share best practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Minister provide details of the outcome of these public consultations, in particular, increasing the minimum legal age for the purchase, possession and use of tobacco in Singapore from 18 to 21 years old?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In addition, are there further plans to increase our support for those who want to quit smoking?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As a former smoker, I know how difficult it is to quit and how quitting made me a Grouchy Smurf for quite a while.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The decision to quit is easy; the ability to follow through is very difficult.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And if we can provide more support, I am sure we will see a higher success rate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will the Ministry, for example, expand and enhance the very successful "I Quit" campaign?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am proud to say that since 12 October 2013, I have remained smoke-free and I am a very happy Papa Smurf now.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Unfortunately, smoking continues to be a significant contributor to the disease burden in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We are familiar with the diseases suffered by smokers and those exposed to second-hand smoke.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also need to transform our healthcare workforce in order to support care transformation that Minister Gan spoke about, so that we can sustainably achieve better health and better care for all.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The positive news is that growth in the healthcare sector will bring many good jobs, clinical and non-clinical, and at different levels, for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These include nurses, therapists, administrative executives and operations managers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Patrick Tay asked what the Ministry is doing to help Singaporeans access these jobs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will support young school leavers to join healthcare.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the past five years, the number of graduates for medical and allied health has generally increased, while the number of graduates for nursing has decreased.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, we have made consistent efforts in the past few years to enhance nursing in terms of career progression, professional development and recognition.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The positive news is that intakes have increased.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH has attracted more students to join nursing programmes in the Institute of Technical Education (ITE), polytechnics and NUS, from 1,500 in 2012 to over 1,800 in 2016.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Overall, our intake for nursing has increased by 20%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to sustain efforts to enhance the attractiveness of nursing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Christopher de Souza suggested that we develop our local allied health professional workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2016, MOH worked with the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) to introduce four degree-level allied health programmes (AHPs) in physiotherapy, occupational therapy, diagnostic radiography and radiation therapy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Two hundred and thirty students were admitted in the first cohort.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This year, SIT will be increasing the number of places for these AHP courses by 30% to 300 students for fresh school leavers and mid-career professionals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I agree with Mr Patrick Tay that we would like to attract more mid-career Singaporeans into healthcare.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH and WSG have established PCPs for mid-career Singaporeans to be trained as registered nurses (RNs) and enrolled nurses (ENs), physiotherapists, occupational therapists and diagnostic radiographers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The latest PCP for dental surgery assistants (DSAs) was launched in November 2016.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since 2003, over 1,000 locals have participated in the Healthcare PCPs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The funding will encourage employers to admit more PCP-trained nurses and enable them to better support these nurses in their transition to a new career.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also tap on MOM's new Attach and Train scheme to enable more mid-career Singaporeans to take up PCP nursing training.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides enhancing the local PCPs, MOH will introduce a new overseas nursing scholarship under the Healthcare Graduate Studies Award (HGSA) for non-nursing degree graduates, including fresh graduates and those with prior work experience.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Awardees can pursue an overseas Graduate Entry Masters (GEM) nursing programme and will join the nursing profession as RNs after their studies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They will be fully sponsored for their nursing course, including tuition fees and maintenance allowances.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We target to give out 20 such nursing scholarships annually.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are also non-clinical roles for PMETs in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our public healthcare clusters will offer administrative and executive positions under WSG's PCP for professional executives, in areas like human resource and hospital operations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Regional Health Systems (RHSes) will be training more mid-career Singaporeans as Care Coordinator Associates, to coordinate the care services required by patients post-discharge and empower patients to manage their conditions well at home.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Several public hospitals have created Basic Care Assistant positions to help nurses provide personal care to patients, such as feeding and transferring.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will free up nurses' time to concentrate on their clinical duties.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will be providing employers with on-the-job training support of $10,000 for each Basic Care Assistant hired.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The public hospitals aim to recruit about 200 Singaporeans for these part-time positions over the next three years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are even more job opportunities in the aged care sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have also improved the designs of nursing homes to provide more greenery and a cosier living environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since 2014, we have also put in place the Enhanced Nursing Home Standards (ENHS) which was developed in consultation with the sector to not only guide consistent, safe and quality care in homes, but also to ensure that the psycho-social needs of residents are met.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH conducts licensing checks to ensure that nursing homes uphold these standards.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We impose measures, such as a shorter licensing period, on nursing homes with severe or repeated non-compliances.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The licensing period of each nursing home is available online for the public's reference.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to support the sector in improving their quality of care, including sharing good practices beyond the enhanced standards amongst providers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But the needs for aged care are not and should not be met by nursing homes alone.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, most Singaporeans prefer to age at home.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, we should work towards making nursing home care an option of last resort.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To achieve this, MOH is strengthening home and community care options to help seniors avoid institutionalisation and age comfortably at home and in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With home care, centre-based care, trained domestic workers and nursing home places, we can adequately support the needs of seniors in 2020 and beyond.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The growth in the aged care sector means we have new job positions for care staff across the island, offering Singaporeans a chance to work closer to home.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2016, AIC helped 400 locals find jobs in the aged care sector through four job fairs, with about 25 participating aged care providers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This year, AIC will enhance the Community Care Traineeship Programme (CCTP), which is a Place and Train programme, by including more structured bite-sized training under the programme to help Singaporeans take up healthcare and therapy assistant roles.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides care staff, the aged care sector will need PMETs to join its workforce to lead the new institutions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mid-career Singaporeans with managerial experience can tap on the Senior Management Associate Scheme (SMAS) to switch careers to the aged care sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, MOH will enhance our "Return to Nursing" programme to encourage non-practising local nurses to rejoin the healthcare sector and, in particular, to take up new positions in the aged care sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi asked about the Ministry's efforts to further develop the nursing profession.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH set up the National Nursing Taskforce in 2012 to strengthen the development of the nursing profession.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have since enhanced professional development, career advancement and recognition for nurses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Going forward, we will have to meet higher healthcare needs with a more constrained workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This challenge would be felt more acutely for the nursing profession as the over 34,000 practising nurses currently form the largest professional group of the healthcare workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Also, nurses are needed to anchor primary and aged care to lead care transformation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Therefore, MOH set up the Future Nursing Career Review Committee in April last year, comprising nursing leaders from across the different care settings.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Committee has identified three strategic areas of focus, namely, Care, Community and Competency, to develop a future-ready nursing workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The first area of focus is job and process redesign to enable nurses to focus more on patient care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We encourage public healthcare institutions to undertake a comprehensive review of nurses' roles so that they can spend more time on direct patient care and take on deeper nursing care roles.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, the Singapore General Hospital (SGH) has introduced a digital nursing handover notes system to minimise the time spent handing over patients' case notes between shifts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Experienced ENs can be trained to take on more complex procedures, such as wound care, administering oral medications and giving subcutaneous and intramuscular injections The second area of focus is to develop community nursing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If we want to go beyond healthcare to health, we need nurses to deliver preventive health in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If we want to go beyond hospitals to the community and home, we need nurses to support patients with good day and home-based care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The RHSes will expand the existing pilot manpower partnership scheme under which they hire and deploy nurses across their community care partners.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: RHSes will also pilot a community nursing team network, comprising nurses and support care staff, to provide seamless care to patients from hospital to home and help seniors age in place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These RHS-level community services and partnerships with community care providers will give nurses greater exposure to different aspects of community nursing for a more diverse career.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will work with the nursing profession to develop Community Nursing as a distinctive career track in its own right, with a comprehensive competency framework that covers the skills needed for different roles in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will underpin a more holistic system of training and deployment of community nurses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will start building a pipeline for nurses to enter the community care sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Community Nursing Scholarship will support students who choose to undergo the nursing diploma or degree courses and offer them clinical attachments with community institutions and work in the community care setting after graduation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They will be further supported to undergo the Advanced Diploma in Community Nursing to gain deeper skills in community nursing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This exposure to community nursing will also become part of the leadership development of nursing leaders so that they will gain competencies across both acute and community care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The third area of focus is on developing competencies to prepare nurses for the future.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A more fundamental review of our nursing training system is needed so that we can better support nurses in developing deeper, future-ready skills in their nursing career.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, we will need to enhance the recognition of the skills and competencies that ENs have acquired at work to facilitate experienced ENs to undertake an accelerated diploma upgrading course to become RNs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For RNs, the Advanced Diploma courses will be reviewed to support more flexible, modularised ways of learning so that more can upgrade themselves.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the next few months, MOH will work with the Healthcare Services Employees' Union and healthcare institutions to engage nurses through focus group discussions to hear more ideas to implement the Committee's recommendations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With these three shifts, nurses can look forward to more meaningful and dynamic careers across the acute and community care sectors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With more time dedicated to direct patient care, nurses can better focus on what they are trained for and what they are passionate about.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Patients can look forward to more integrated care and care within the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Beyond nursing, we are working to build a future-ready healthcare workforce across all healthcare professions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH is collaborating with SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) to develop a Skills Framework for the healthcare sector to support healthcare workers in their professional and career development.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH is working closely with MSF to ensure that the Skills Framework is applicable to their counterparts in the social service sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will further develop the capabilities of our pharmacy workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Last year, we implemented the National Pharmacy Residency Programme to train specialist pharmacists, with a total of 15 residents enrolled to date.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, we are developing advanced pharmacy practitioners through the Advanced Practice Competency Framework for Pharmacists.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This framework serves as a developmental tool for pharmacists to gear towards advanced level competencies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To upskill our pharmacy technicians, we developed the SkillsFuture Earn and Learn Programme leading to an Advanced Diploma in Pharmaceutical Sciences in collaboration with Nanyang Polytechnic.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This 18-month structured work-learn programme aims to enhance core competencies of pharmacy technicians so that they can take on bigger roles.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Training for the first batch is slated to start in April this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even as we grow and develop our healthcare workforce to meet current and future needs, we recognise that with a shrinking local labour force, we will need to supplement our core local healthcare workforce with foreign manpower.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The proportion of foreign doctors has decreased from 18% in end 2012.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will work to help our foreign workforce assimilate to the local environment to meet our healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Dr Chia Shi-Lu mentioned, it is also important to ensure that good staff are retained.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Through various efforts, we have reduced our public healthcare staff attrition rate from 10.1% to 8.4% between 2012 and 2016.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Attrition for nurses has decreased from 8.4% in 2012 to 6.5% in 2016.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But the formal workforce is only one part of our care system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Caregivers play just as, if not a more important role, in our healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about our plans to support caregivers of seniors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have expanded home and centre-based care services, as well as respite care services, including weekend respite at our SCCs, where caregivers can place their loved ones to be cared for, while they run errands or take a short break.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: AIC also started a three-year pilot since September 2015 to embed more comprehensive caregiver support services within five SCCs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These include supporting caregivers' emotional and psycho-social needs and assisting them with information and referral services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For caregivers requiring further assistance, the SCCs will also link them to a central pool of social work support.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: AIC has also rolled out AICareLinks at five hospitals and at its office at Maxwell Road.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These are one-stop counters where caregivers can receive advice on services and schemes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Caregivers can also call AIC's Singapore Silver Line to receive assistance over the phone.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also provide an annual training grant of $200 for caregivers of seniors and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH is also leveraging technology to care for seniors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have started several pilots on senior monitoring using technology in Yuhua, Bedok and Marine Parade.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under the Community Network for Seniors pilot in Tampines, Eastern Health Alliance is piloting a call centre service called "Careline" to support seniors living alone.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Seniors enrolled in the service can call the Careline should they need help.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Careline will also make regular calls to seniors and provide them with useful health information.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In line with Dr Lily Neo's suggestion, we are also working with MND and HDB to study new forms of housing and care options for seniors to age-in-place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Ms Tin Pei Ling, as well as Mr Dennis Tan and Ms Joan Pereira, asked about support for mental health.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will further strengthen care in the community over the next five years in five ways.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, to improve the early identification of mental health symptoms, frontline staff of selected Government agencies, such as HDB, the Singapore Police Force (SPF), the National Environment Agency (NEA), community partners and social service agencies, will receive basic training on mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They will be trained to identify and respond to persons with mental health issues in the community, such as referring these persons to AIC for help.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also continue to create more Dementia-Friendly Communities (DFCs), where residents, businesses and other partners are trained to identify and assist seniors with dementia.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, we will strengthen our response to mental health needs in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: AIC will act as a "first responder" to mental health needs identified in the community and coordinate care across the health and social sectors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Community partners and caregivers looking after persons with mental health needs may call the Singapore Silver Line (SSL) or email for assistance and support.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Third, we will expand mental health and dementia services in polyclinics to make care more accessible.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our target is for one in two polyclinics to implement mental health clinics by 2021.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Fourth, MOH and MSF will work together to strengthen integrated health and social care services in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will increase the number of allied health community intervention teams from 14 to 18 by financial year (FY) 2021, to support GPs, community and grassroots organisations in caring for persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will resource IMH to widen their case management support so that more IMH patients will be supported in the post-discharge period and transit well back home.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As we move beyond healthcare to health, we need to do more to tackle factors that contribute to ill-health and diseases.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Tobacco use is one such major contributor in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: HPB has a programme called "I Quit" that supports smokers to quit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will extend the programme's outreach through roadshows at various community and workplace settings this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We want to protect our young from the harms of tobacco and lay the foundations for good health.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In Singapore, nearly half or 45% of smokers become regular smokers between the ages of 18 and 21.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: According to a report by the World Health Organisation (WHO), persons who do not start smoking before the age of 21 "are unlikely to ever begin".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Findings from Needham, Massachusetts, the first US town to increase its minimum legal age (MLA) for sale of tobacco from 18 to 21, are promising.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Youth smoking rates have fallen more rapidly here, compared to neighbouring areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At least 215 localities in the US, including New York City and the states of Hawaii and California, have since increased their MLA to 21.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Between December 2015 and March 2016, HPB conducted public consultation on further tobacco control measures.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The feedback showed considerable support for raising the MLA in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The change will be phased in over a few years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are taking steps towards standardising tobacco packaging.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Australia, France and the UK have all implemented standardised packaging.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, you have three cuts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This will help MOH stay ahead of future demand and provide better care to keep our residents in better health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Next, more broadly, primary care has to be the bedrock of a healthcare system, especially with an ageing population.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MOH tell us how it plans to strengthen primary care nationwide so that more patients can be managed in the community more effectively?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Will these networks link up with nursing homes, VWOs and other agencies like MSF's Social Service Offices, to provide more holistic care across the patient's journey in the community?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As a doctor and as the son of a cancer patient, I have seen first-hand how important palliative care can be for adult patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That need is even more crucial when the patient on palliative care is a child, a child with life-limiting illness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The child may not understand what is going on and the parents will need that extra support.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For the parents, the journey is heartbreaking when the child has a life-limiting illness.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Nonetheless, we need to persist with our efforts as a community, together with our health professionals, to raise palliative care awareness.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We should encourage more dialogues to destigmatise end-of-life issues so that the early conversations can better inform care planning.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Will the Ministry share an update about the public education initiatives to increase awareness about Advanced Care Planning (ACP), palliative care and end-of-life issues?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How will MOH work with VWOs to improve public awareness of the accessibility and types of palliative care available?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: For many families, increasingly, spouses and adult children are working full-time and need palliative care support for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Will we be able to meet the demands for hospices and home palliative services?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Will MOH be able to train enough qualified personnel to cope with the rising demand due to our ageing population?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Will the Minister share how funding and MediSave uses will be augmented to meet this need?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: AIC can support and help caregivers find closure when the loved ones pass on, so that they, usually family members, will not go into a depressive state.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Would the Ministry elaborate on the available support for the bereaved, especially those from our vulnerable groups, such as caregivers with low incomes or little family support?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: In this overseas study by Wenger and colleagues, no relation to the football manager, Swiss doctors spent less than one-third of their time on direct patient care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: The rest was used up by paperwork and administrative duties.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: What measures is MOH taking to reduce paperwork and administration for doctors, nurses and healthcare workers?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Furthermore, in the design of hospital wards and clinics, is MOH looking at economy of movement, making sure that staff do not have to move around more than necessary, making sure computer systems simplify rather than complicate?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: This can help our healthcare workers spend more time, and more quality time, with patients in better communication, better engagement, better care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: It is also a people- and patient-centric one, utilising the encounter-based delivery model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: However, just doing our best and working very hard may not be good enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: As healthcare organisations face unprecedented challenges to enhance quality, productivity, reduce harm, improve access and efficiency, eliminate waste and lower cost, innovation and technology have to become a focus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: It may require some shift in mindsets to implement new organisational models, service delivery and customer relations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The Harvard Business Review states that 65% of healthcare interactions will be mobile by 2018.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Investments in consumer-facing mobile apps, wearable technology, remote monitoring devices, virtual care and big data analytics will become common practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Data-driven healthcare creates a tremendous potential to make every care environment a data-driven learning environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How is MOH utilising data-driven healthcare to help formulate guidelines and policies and set new relevant key performance indicators (KPIs)?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: I strongly feel that across the continuum from primary to tertiary care, there is, indeed, room for a concerted effort to revamp, relook, review, reconnect and reinvent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: At the end of the day, it is really about the smart balance of technology, both the digital and the human touch.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Gan Kim Yong has highlighted key shifts in our healthcare system to help build a sustainable healthcare system for Singaporeans in the future.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will focus on how we are working to implement the "3 Beyonds" − beyond hospital to community, beyond quality to value, and beyond healthcare to health – in laying the foundation for a healthier future.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This river is the source of life as it provides food and water to the people living along it.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, the inhabitants up-river are dumping waste into the river polluting the water downstream.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Villagers staying down-river are falling ill as a result of bathing in and drinking the polluted water.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It can invest substantial resources researching the health effects of polluted water or put lots of money into expensive technological solutions to treat and purify the water.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It can also look for alternative sources of drinking water.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: All these options would translate into long-term commitment of time and resources in managing the consequences of a real problem.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, the underlying root cause has not gone away.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Alternatively, the affected village can work with the inhabitants upstream to identify and remove the source of pollution into the river.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This would definitely help address the real problem, without having to resort to expensive and complex solutions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Yes, this upstream approach is one of the fundamental shifts that Minister Gan has alluded to in his speech − beyond healthcare to health.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Besides advocating health promotion in the general population, our focus now has shifted even more upstream to target Singaporeans as young as possible, from the preschool ages.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The foundation of a healthier future is in our children and youth.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There is strong evidence that good habits start from young, and these continue to reap benefits in healthier lifestyles and choices into adulthood.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: (In Mandarin):   Good health will lay a good foundation for the holistic development of our children and youths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, we are now seeing several new trends, such as more frequent use of electronic gadgets, easy access to high-calorie food and drinks, and increasingly sedentary behaviour.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Therefore, we need to look into nurturing healthier children and youths in a sustainable way.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will equip young Singaporeans, their parents, caregivers and teachers to help our children and youths lead a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: NurtureSG will focus on the greater engagement of parents by equipping them with relevant knowledge and parenting skills so that they can play an active role in providing a health-promoting home environment for their children.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition, the physical and social environments are key determinants of health, particularly for children who are in the early stages of development.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Hence, NurtureSG will also focus on fostering active and healthy living in the school and the community so as to integrate health promotion into the daily activities of our young.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In order to deepen and strengthen health education in educational institutions, we will provide more opportunities for children and youths to be more active in physical activities and have access to healthier meal options.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will help them understand the importance of quality sleep and enhance their socio-emotional skills so that they stay healthy, both physically and mentally.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As long as we all work together, I believe we can raise awareness of the importance of good health amongst young Singaporeans and create a healthier future for them.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: (In English): We announced the plans for NurtureSG two weeks ago.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And we will do so through two enablers: through parents, who are role models in shaping the attitudes and behaviours of our children, and through the school and community.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Janil had elaborated during the MOE COS the various initiatives that mainstream schools will be embarking on to address these three focus areas.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will now share with Members what we will do in going further upstream to target children of preschool ages.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With regard to the nutrition of our preschoolers, let me share an example of how the HPB's Healthy Meals in Childcare Centres Programme (HMCCP) contributes to our vision of "Healthy Meals for Every Child".

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since 2015, she has been attending Agape Little Uni @ Sengkang, which participates in HMCCP.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Raenelle has grown to love healthier food and is a health ambassador in her home.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As a result, her mother, Regina, has adopted healthier cooking methods, such as steaming and stir-frying at home, and also taking right meal portions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And when they shop for groceries, they look for healthier food options contributing to a balanced diet.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Although certain healthy food options can be slightly more expensive, there is also a wide variety of affordable alternatives labelled with the Healthier Choice Symbol (HCS).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: By making the right choices, Raenelle and Regina are on track towards a healthier future.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also have plans to teach our young to manage themselves well, by equipping preschool educators with the knowledge and understanding of socio-emotional development in young children.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last but not least, we want to raise awareness on the importance and benefits of adequate and quality sleep.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A lack of sleep is associated with impaired cognition, obesity and an increased risk of mental health issues.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, parents who establish regular sleep patterns for children and reduce the amount of screen time for computers, television or mobile phones before sleep, will go a long way towards ensuring quality sleep and better physical and mental health for their children.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To Dr Chia Shi-Lu's queries on Nurture SG, the initiative will benefit our children and young from preschool to IHLs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The respective agencies will be supporting the respective recommendations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, as this is a multi-year ongoing effort and builds on top of existing efforts on child health, it is more meaningful to focus on the programmes and on an overall budget.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As reported in HPB's student health survey in 2015, one in six of our Secondary 1 to Secondary 5, junior colleges and centralised institute students do not eat breakfast at all.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is of concern and we hope that Nurture SG's plans will better guide our youths to live a healthier life.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Gan has spoken about the War on Diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will now focus on the clinical management of diabetes and the development and implementation of evidence-based clinical and lifestyle management of the disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This work is led by a Disease Management Workgroup under the National Diabetes Prevention and Care Taskforce set up in July last year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Good clinical management of diabetes is important, as poorly controlled blood sugars can lead to multiple complications in the long term, such as diabetic retinopathy, limb amputations and chronic kidney disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Early detection and treatment can prevent or slow down the progression of diabetes-related kidney disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2011, the National University Hospital (NUH) and the National Healthcare Group Polyclinics developed the Nephrology Evaluation, Management and Optimisation programme (NEMO).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The pilot programme initiates and optimises kidney protective medication for suitable patients showing early signs of kidney disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As of September 2016, about one-third enrolled on the programme demonstrated improvements, while over 60% maintained stable kidney function.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These positive outcomes give us confidence to scale this initiative nationwide.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will call it "HALT-CKD", which stands for Holistic Approach in Lowering and Tracking Chronic Kidney Disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The new national programme will benefit more patients nationwide and will be implemented progressively at all polyclinics.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Gan also spoke about the setting up of the Agency for Care Effectiveness (or ACE).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will help clinicians and patients alike achieve value, beyond quality, in the area of drugs and healthcare technology, which will support our War on Diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To better equip our primary care doctors to care for diabetic patients, we will roll out two Appropriate Care Guides (ACGs) in July this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The first care guide will provide recommendations on medications for type 2 diabetes and, the second, a systematic way to manage pre-diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: ACE also recently evaluated two classes of patented diabetic drugs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One of them was found to be significantly more cost-effective.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Arising from this, MOH will be listing the drug from the more cost-effective group under the Medication Assistance Fund (MAF), and eligible patients can apply for financial support for this drug.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Patients themselves also have a vital role to play to achieve optimal control of diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The key to managing diabetes starts with taking active steps to lead a healthier lifestyle and to comply with treatment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To better support patients, we are developing a framework to empower them to initiate and sustain lifestyle changes and enhance treatment adherence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Diabetic patients are also best managed when anchored in meaningful doctor-patient relationships in the community.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Primary care is the bedrock of our healthcare system and the key to enabling the shift to bring healthcare beyond hospitals into the community.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is an integral component in our transformative efforts to bring patient-focused care closer to home.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Currently, only 20% of our primary care attendances are in polyclinics, the remainder are with private GPs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is also reflective of where our primary care doctors practise today.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Eighty percent of our primary care doctors are private GPs and a small number of them provide medical care in nursing homes and home medical services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Within primary care, we are also seeing an increase in attendances with chronic medical conditions, like diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, rising from 18% in 2010 to about 27% today.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: PCNs are made up of GPs who are organised into virtual networks and deliver care through a multidisciplinary team of doctors and nurses to manage patients' needs more holistically and effectively.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Patients will benefit from nurse counsellors who will provide individualised advice to better manage their conditions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition, diabetic patients will be able to access diabetic foot and eye screening services more conveniently at the PCN GP clinics, allowing for early detection and treatment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Through PCNs, GPs also have greater scale to link up with community providers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef suggested strengthening primary care to manage patients in the community and better streamlining of care coordination across care settings.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The RHSes and public healthcare institutions have care coordination programmes and care coordinators for patients with multiple needs and frequent hospitalisations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: PCN care coordinators would also be able to spend more time evaluating care needs holistically and refer these patients to the appropriate channels of social assistance, including VWOs and MSF's Social Service Offices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The team-based arrangement will also facilitate like-minded GPs in cross-sharing and peer learning of best practices across PCNs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH will provide GPs participating in PCNs with funding and administrative support to implement team-based care to better track the care outcomes and monitor patients more closely.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Funding support will also be available to enable GPs to better care for patients with complex chronic conditions, such as diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since 2012, he has been utilising the PCN services at Dr Chong's clinic, which gives him access to ancillary services, such as diabetic foot and eye screenings.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I really appreciate them." I am happy to note that Mr Mohd's efforts in leading a healthy lifestyle, coupled with holistic chronic disease management by the PCN team, have helped him to manage his chronic conditions optimally.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Beyond PCNs, MOH will also continue to renew our primary care infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As announced last year, two new FMCs in Keat Hong and Tampines will be operational early this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In particular, Tampines FMC will be located at the integrated complex, Our Tampines Hub, together with a Community Health Centre (CHC) and an SCC, providing our patients with a range of comprehensive community care options.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Residents in Jurong West and Punggol can also look forward to the opening of Pioneer and Punggol polyclinics this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are on track to operationalise new polyclinics in Bukit Panjang, Eunos and Sembawang by 2020.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I am also pleased to announce that we will build a new polyclinic in the Kallang/Balestier area which is expected to be operational by 2020.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also working with the polyclinic groups to refresh the existing polyclinics, to evolve the polyclinics according to changing care needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Polyclinics have progressively been renovated and expanded over the years.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng had asked if Clementi Polyclinic can be expanded.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Expansion plans are already being planned for Clementi Polytechnic and are expected to be completed by next year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry is also looking into partner arrangements to better care for patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since June 2014, Clementi Polyclinic has worked with NUHS-Frontier FMC to transfer over 6,700 patients from Clementi Polyclinic to Frontier FMC for primary care needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked for the progress of the review of PHMCA.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While PHMCA has served us well in ensuring the delivery of safe and quality care, more IT-enabled interventions and mobile services have emerged in recent years.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We need to ensure adequate standards for these services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is important that our healthcare laws stay current and flexible to allow for these shifts in models of care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I announced the revision of PHMCA in October 2016.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since then, we have actively engaged stakeholders, including hospitals and clinics, in focus group discussions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have also engaged patient groups and members of the public to see how we can better ensure patient safety, welfare and continuity of care through the new Healthcare Services Act.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To date, we have held 11 Advisory Panel Discussion sessions and 34 Focus Group Discussion sessions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Both providers and the public have welcomed changes to license healthcare providers by services rather than by premises.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They have also been supportive of changes aimed at making healthcare costs more transparent through the display of fees, more targeted financial counselling and bill itemisation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Requirements to increase the accountability of healthcare providers and clinical oversight over more complex services have been generally positive.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Various providers and members of the public gave useful suggestions on how we can enhance continuity of care for patients through an integrated NEHR.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There are currently security measures in place and my Ministry will continue to strengthen the measures to address these concerns.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We welcome all healthcare service providers and members of the public to review the Bill and provide us with more feedback and suggestions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Healthy lifestyle habits keep chronic diseases at bay.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Staying connected to a regular doctor with improved access to healthcare services within the community will allow for better care management.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH will continue to review our system and ensure that it evolves to ensure a safe delivery of appropriate care to patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I urge all Singaporeans and healthcare providers to partner us in our initiatives to build a healthier future for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng and Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef that we need to raise healthcare productivity through innovation and process improvements to deliver quality care and better value for our patients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our public healthcare institutions did a successful pilot where selected patients with conditions like back pain can be directly referred by their polyclinic doctors for subsidised physiotherapy services, without having to go through a specialist.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This improves patients' access to physiotherapy services and reduces unnecessary delays and referrals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also allows the specialists to focus on other patients who require their services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH will work with our healthcare institutions to look at other areas where we can apply this approach to encourage right-siting and effective use of healthcare resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng is right that we need to reduce administrative work for healthcare professionals so that they can focus on patient care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With this in mind, NUH reviewed its processes for documenting patient information and replaced hardcopy forms with electronic ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will look at further measures to cut down the administrative load for our healthcare workers across the healthcare system, including doing away with unnecessary surveys and form-filling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Tan also asked about the design of hospital wards and clinics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is scope to further improve productivity through clever use of design and technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes doing time-motion studies to monitor operational workflows and finding ways to optimise the processes and reduce inefficiencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Technology is a key enabler in our efforts to improve productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our strategy for technology is three-pronged: digitise, connect, analyse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, our institutions need to digitise their information and processes to provide healthcare professionals the information they need for decision-making.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, we are strengthening connections across IT systems to facilitate the exchange of information, especially across different clusters and institutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes linkages with VWOs and private sector providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, we are analysing the healthcare data collected to better predict care needs and utilisation patterns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, using data to identify and reach out to seniors who visit hospitals regularly to see how their healthcare needs can be better met through community and home care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our healthcare professionals are well-trained and dedicated, often going the extra mile to look after their patients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I also want to acknowledge the strong support from Ms Thanaletchimi and our brothers and sisters from the Healthcare Services Employees’ Union (HSEU) and thank them for their valuable feedback and active participation in improving our healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH greatly appreciates our partnership with the union.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By working together as trusted partners, we increase our chances of success and shorten the time we need to reach our goals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Earlier this year, I launched the Philips Health Continuum Space in Toa Payoh.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The company is now focusing on health-related products as a core business, bringing together expertise from different fields, including design and engineering.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The innovation facility is a living lab for healthcare professionals to collaborate, co-create and test out healthcare solutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am glad that Philips is interested to work with local small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and startups to use this facility and also to test-bed their solutions in the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our startups are also providing innovative solutions to tackle healthcare-related challenges in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling spoke about using digital technology to enhance eldercare.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Home-grown company Jaga-Me offers "home care on demand" to give patients and their families access to professional home nursing and caregiving services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are a group of young Singaporeans who are keen to make a difference in improving lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another technology solution is T-Rehab, where patients carry out physiotherapy exercises at home using wearable sensors, with their progress monitored remotely by physiotherapists.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I encourage our healthcare institutions to work with startups like Jaga-Me and T-Rehab to support their innovations and use these new ideas to help transform our healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The key is to have an environment where we can try new ideas and fail safely so that we can learn from these failures and continue to innovate by pushing the boundaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is also a key focus for the War on Diabetes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza has asked for an update.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For Season Two of the National Steps Challenge, participants have hit key milestones more quickly than Season One.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One hundred and fifty thousand people clocked 10,000 steps or more on at least five days per week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To step up the momentum, HPB has been working with SportSG to scale up popular programmes like Sundays @ The Park, Sunrise in the City and Fitness@Work to increase the variety of activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When it comes to preventing and managing diabetes, diet is a critical factor.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While the decision and responsibility to eat healthily rest with the individual, MOH will continue to work with our partners to foster a supportive environment for Singaporeans to make healthy food choices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have increased availability of healthier meals in restaurants, food courts and hawker centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: HPB works closely with industry players through the Healthier Dining Programme and HCS programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With MOE's support, schools can only sell packaged drinks with lower sugar content of less than 6%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is important to help our children adopt healthy habits from young.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I applaud the People's Association for their initiative to cater healthier foods at grassroots events since December 2016.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have also done this for my constituency events and received positive feedback from my residents who appreciate our efforts to provide them with healthier meals and healthier snacks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We want to provide tasty healthier choices for our public officers and guests so that they can enjoy the food while staying healthy and active.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: HPB has been working on this important area over the last few years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The aim is to go upstream in the food manufacturing process, to increase the proportion of whole grains and healthier oils served in restaurants, food courts and hawker centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through this scheme, consumers can benefit from a wider variety of healthier meals, to help prevent and manage diabetes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Food manufacturing is one of Singapore's strengths, and our manufacturers are recognised worldwide for the quality and taste of their products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By working closely with the industry, I am confident we can further enhance the sector's value-add by developing healthier products which taste just as delicious and riding on the trusted Singapore brand to expand our markets overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am encouraged to see more Singaporeans switching to healthier choices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Companies have also reformulated their products to reduce the amount of salt, oil and sugar so that they can qualify for HCS certification.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, there are over 2,500 HCS products available across 70 food categories, compared to just 300 products when HCS started in 2001.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The sale of HCS products has been growing at 9% annually, compared to 2% to 3% for other food products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While Singaporeans are eating more healthily, we are still consuming too much sugar.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On average, Singaporeans consume 12 teaspoons of sugar daily, more than the five teaspoons limit recommended by WHO.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also see a worrying trend of children and youths consuming more sugar-sweetened beverages (SSB) than before.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Compared to food, SSBs are easy to over-consume as they do not provide a sense of fullness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many are also low in nutrients and are essentially "empty calories".

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In Singapore, SSBs contribute 60% of our total sugar intake, higher than many other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Two-thirds of this sugar come from pre-packaged SSBs, such as soft drinks and packet drinks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Other countries have implemented a range of measures targeted at lowering SSB consumption to reduce obesity and chronic diseases like diabetes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Diabetes Taskforce has obtained views from industry players and individuals on how to reduce sugar consumption in Singapore, including from pre-packaged SSBs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We studied the practices in other countries, which include regulatory measures like soda tax, warning labels for high-sugar drinks and advertising restrictions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chen Show Mao has also highlighted some of these examples.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also continue to monitor the situation in other countries to assess the effectiveness of the measures that they have implemented in changing dietary preferences and consumer behaviours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: NGOs and VWOs are important partners for MOH.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In our War on Diabetes, we work with the Diabetic Society of Singapore (DSS) and Touch Community Services in areas, such as diabetes education, patient and caregiver support and disease management.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We work with and support the work of NGOs in different ways, such as funding them to provide services, extending seed funding for them to experiment with new ideas and collaborating with them through our RHSes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For SIBs, some observers have noted the benefits, including those which Mr Perera highlighted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Others saw downsides, such as the complex negotiations among multiple parties, resulting in delays and high transaction costs and possible diversion of attention and resources away from important causes which are less measurable and harder to achieve outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In some countries, SIBs are used out of financial necessity due to insufficient public budget to support certain social programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore is fortunate to be in a stronger fiscal position, thanks to our stable political system and the Government which has been planning long term and spending prudently within our means.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to study different ways of funding and working with NGOs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ultimately, regardless of the funding arrangement, what we need are collective action and strong partnerships among the Government, NGOs, industry players, communities and individuals to win the war on diabetes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another important area is to encourage early and regular health screening.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For diabetes, the current arrangement is for Singaporeans aged 40 and above to go for screening every three years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are also other factors, such as family history, body mass index and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: DRA is an evidence-based, self-administered questionnaire to assess an individual's diabetes risk.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will offer these services to them for free as a special benefit for our Pioneer Generation (PG).

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The fixed fee of $2 and $5 will cover both the initial screening and the first post-screening consultation, if the test results show that a consultation is required.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We want to reduce the drop-off rate of someone who is tested positive but does not follow-up to see a doctor for post-screening consultation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through these enhancements, we hope that more Singaporeans will go for screening, including those who face higher risks of getting diabetes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Early detection and intervention are important in preventing diabetes and managing the disease.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This has also been raised by other Members in the past, most recently by Ms Cheng Li Hui in October 2016.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our vaccination subsidy policies are guided by recommendations from the Expert Committee on Immunisation (ECI).

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a committee which comprises specialists from public and private healthcare institutions in infectious diseases, microbiology, paediatrics and public health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ECI will assess a vaccine based on factors, such as the burden of the disease in Singapore, safety and efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of the vaccine.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Vaccinations, such as measles and diphtheria, are subsidised to achieve sufficient population immunity to prevent community outbreaks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For pneumococcal disease, the risk of an outbreak is currently assessed to be low.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our incidence of serious invasive pneumococcal disease in Singapore is also lower than other countries, such as the US and Australia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hence, the Committee has recommended a targeted approach for specific high-risk groups, such as children below five, seniors above 65 and individuals with chronic medical conditions, such as diabetes, asthma and heart diseases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are also generous Government grants via the Baby Bonus cash gift and the Child Development Account which can be used for pneumococcal vaccination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH has been increasing our support for this sector over the past years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked how MOH is working with VWOs to improve public awareness, quality and accessibility of palliative care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will work with community providers to reach out to the public through different channels, including using art as one of the ways to reach out to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Alongside such efforts, MOH will work with the Singapore Hospice Council on a structured three-year initiative to promote public understanding of palliative care, including how we can better support caregivers during grief and bereavement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: An important initiative is to help Singaporeans plan ahead for their care preferences through ACP, together with their loved ones and their care team.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We aim to reach out to 25,000 Singaporeans over the next four years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH will work with our community partners, RHSes and AIC to expand ACP in different care settings, such as specialist outpatient clinics and primary care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another area is to increase the capacity, accessibility and quality of palliative care services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I recently visited Assisi Hospice again and they have a new building with 85 palliative beds, including five beds for paediatric palliative care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are also increasing their home palliative care services to about 1,000 patients each year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The palliative care workforce has also increased by 50% from 2011 to 2016.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With the added capacity, more Singaporeans with terminal illnesses can benefit from palliative care services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are working with the Singapore Hospice Council to launch a quality improvement programme for palliative care providers, to maintain high quality standards as we increase our capacity in this sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To further enhance home palliative care services, our RHSes will work with community providers and VWOs to pilot integrated home palliative care programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under these programmes, patients can receive medical and nursing care at home, as well as assistance in their daily activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Patients requiring short inpatient stays will be cared for in community hospitals, before they return home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng on the need to support children with life-limiting illnesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is a difficult time for families which are facing this situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Committee has engaged different groups of stakeholders, such as caregivers, service providers, insurers and members of the public, through focus group discussions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will continue to consult widely to gather further views and feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To sum up, MOH will focus on three key shifts for the next few years: beyond healthcare to health, beyond hospital to community, and beyond quality to value.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to grow a future-ready healthcare workforce and strengthen primary and community care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will achieve these outcomes by working in partnership with communities, healthcare institutions, companies and unions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our goal, Madam, is to help all Singaporeans achieve better health, better care and a better life.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Well, we have a bit of time for clarifications.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: First, the Minister mentioned that the reorganisation of the clusters is to enable us to pursue care transformation and, I quote, "more effectively and decisively".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: We note that the RHSes have also been in existence for a few years.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: So, could I just ask: what are some of the achievements of the RHSes when they were around?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The second clarification is for Senior Minister of State Amy Khor.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I just wanted a quick question about whether the Senior Minister of State could say something about initiatives to improve the health of women and what more is being planned in terms of women healthcare.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: For Minister of State Chee, on productivity, we have been talking a lot about aged care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I was just wondering if there has been maybe equal at least, even additional emphasis, on productivity in the aged care sector and how the Ministry is encouraging manpower effectiveness in this sector, given that we can expect a lot more demand for manpower in the future.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: And for Minister of State Lam, yes, last year, he mentioned about the one-doctor-one-patient initiative in the context of primary care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I was wondering what has the progress been on that particular front?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: When we first set up the RHSes, they had a very clear mission, that is, to integrate care in the respective regions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The RHSes have since worked very hard to establish collaborations and partnerships with the regional service providers so that we can integrate care at the regional level and reach out to the population within the region.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over the last few years, they have done exactly that.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This has also provided the impetus for the RHSes to be innovative, test out new models of care and provide the diversity needed for the healthcare system to evolve and to develop.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, we are moving towards the three key shifts and this is why we are bringing the RHSes together so that they can leverage one another's strengths.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over the last few years, they have spent a lot of effort and invested heavily in community engagement.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They have worked very well with the nursing homes in the area.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With the GPs, they have the GPFirst programme.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They will bring this experience in engaging the community players to SingHealth when they eventually come together and merge with SingHeatlh.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are leveraging the experience and knowledge that they have developed to help the integrated clusters move forward in a decisive and effective manner.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, I want to thank Dr Chia Shi-Lu for speaking in the interest of women and I must acknowledge that actually Dr Lily Neo also asked about women's health in her cut earlier.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, let me say that women's health is an important priority for Singapore simply because they face significant health losses due to the various disease groups that affect them, as well as the fact that, of course, they have a longer life expectancy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Dr Lily Neo says, they now still spend the longer life years in disability.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Women's Health Advisory Committee, now known as the Women's Health Committee, was established in 2012.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This programme has morphed into a workplace grant for companies with particular programmes that they can pick up.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The others will be outreach into the community through health talks, for instance, through HPB, as well as we have a women's health calendar that we have been publishing for many years, and in the vernacular also, to reach out to women.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently, we are promoting women's health in three aspects: firstly, is continuation of promoting breast cancer screening as well as follow-up through new outreach programmes and campaigns.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The other one is on bone health, so we are targeting campaigns working towards World Osteoporosis Day, with targeted campaigns to raise awareness among women about the importance of bone health from young, not just for women in the older age groups.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The third one, I am pleased to announce, is in support of diabetes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also working with the public hospitals to promote greater awareness about gestational diabetes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And that is important because studies have shown that, if you pick them early, then it will help to reduce complications during pregnancy as well as reduce the risk of having type-2 diabetes for the mother and child later on through preventive programmes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: HPB will also be designing and developing a mobile pregnancy app on HealthHub for pregnant women so that they can monitor their blood pressure level, blood sugar level as well as the body mass index (BMI).

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition to that, we will also be reaching out through the community to raise awareness about Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) and to get people who had GDM to take preventive measures to reduce their risk of type-2 diabetes developing later on.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We also want to do this for primary care, step-down care and ILTC as well as for community care.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is something which we want to do throughout the entire healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For aged care, for example, there are a few things we have worked together with the providers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In areas, such as cleaning, how do we have equipment and technology that can allow them to do cleaning in a more efficient and more productive manner, one that will require less manpower?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The manpower challenges they face are actually similar to the manpower challenges that are faced by our acute healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The second area is that we also want to see what we can do to multiply the impact that our healthcare workers can make.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
